key_features.classic_presentation: ONSET: ACUTE onset over hours to days. More common in elderly, institutionalized, or chronic constipation patients. LOCATION: Left lower quadrant (LLQ) or diffuse lower abdomen. DURATION: CONSTANT pain lasting hours to days. CHARACTER: CRAMPY, COLICKY pain initially, becoming CONSTANT and SEVERE if ischemia develops. AGGRAVATING: Eating or drinking worsens distension and pain. RELIEVING: NOTHING relieves pain. Vomiting may provide brief relief of distension. TIMING: Initially INTERMITTENT crampy pain, becomes CONSTANT as obstruction persists. SEVERITY: 6-9/10, moderate to severe. ASSOCIATED SYMPTOMS: Marked abdominal distension (asymmetric), absolute constipation (obstipation), inability to pass flatus, nausea and vomiting (may be feculent if prolonged). Tympanic distended abdomen. KEY POSITIVES: Massive asymmetric distension, obstipation, elderly patient, chronic constipation history. KEY NEGATIVES: Ability to pass large amounts of flatus or stool rules out complete obstruction.

includes.patient_friendly: lower left side around your groin

red_flags: Sudden severe pain with rigid abdomen - perforation with peritonitis, call 911
Fever with severe pain - ischemic or necrotic bowel
Hypotension or altered mental status - septic shock, call 911
Bloody or dark red stools - mucosal ischemia
